mainTopic: The meaning of the פסוק ״וְאֵלָיו הוּא נֹשֵׂא אֶת נַפְשׁוֹ״ (דברים 24:15) about paying a שכיר on time, and the מחלוקת between רב הונא and רב חסדא over whose soul is taken when wages are held back.
overview: The גמרא explains how the other Sage uses the פסוק ״וְאֵלָיו הוּא נֹשֵׂא אֶת נַפְשׁוֹ״: a worker risks his life for his wages, so you must not hold them back. A second reading says withholding wages is like taking a soul. רב הונא and רב חסדא argue whether this means the robber's soul or the victim's soul, and each explains the other's פסוק from משלי. The גמרא then returns to the משנה. The employer violates the prohibition only if the worker asked for his pay, and a ברייתא learns from ״אִתְּךָ״ that he must also have the money and must not have sent the worker to a storekeeper or money changer. רב ששת and רבה argue whether, after such a transfer, the worker can still go back to the employer to collect. Next, רב ששת rules that an employer who hires a contractor does violate בל תלין. This connects to the question of whether a craftsman owns the improvement he adds to an item. A ברייתא about a garment given to a craftsman is offered as support for רב ששת. רב מרי pushes it aside by reading it as the cleaning of a coarse garment. When that is challenged, the גמרא defends him by reading it as a worker paid for each tread, who is a regular hired worker.

steps.title: What does the other Sage learn from this verse?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the second Sage uses the פסוק that the first Sage used for his own derivation.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other Sage, what does he do with this verse?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question: the other Sage did not use this פסוק the way the first one did, so what does he learn from it? This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a rule that no words in the תורה are extra. If one Sage did not use ״וְאֵלָיו הוּא נֹשֵׂא אֶת נַפְשׁוֹ״ for the earlier teaching, he must use it for something else. The גמרא wants to know what that is.

keyTerms.meaning: And the other one (the other Sage). A standard way to ask how the other opinion handles a source.

phrases.english: And the other one?
phrases.notes: He's asking: what does the other Sage learn from this פסוק, since he didn't use it for the earlier teaching?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up from the earlier discussion of the two Sages' derivations.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the second Sage learns from ״וְאֵלָיו הוּא נֹשֵׂא אֶת נַפְשׁוֹ״.

steps.title: The worker risks his life for his wages
steps.stepSummary: The other Sage uses the פסוק for a ברייתא: the worker risked his life to earn this money, so it must not be held back.
steps.simpleTranslation: That verse is needed for what a ברייתא teaches: "For he sets his soul upon it." Why did this worker climb a ramp, hang from a tree, and put himself in danger of death? Wasn't it for his wages?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the other Sage uses the פסוק as a reason why paying a שכיר on time is so serious. The worker puts his life at risk to earn that money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words ״נֹשֵׂא אֶת נַפְשׁוֹ״ are read as "he risks his life" for the pay. That turns the פסוק into a moral argument. Someone who risked his life for his wages should not have to wait for them.

keyTerms.meaning: He needs it (the פסוק) for a different teaching.
A ramp or tall incline that is dangerous to climb.

phrases.english: That verse is needed for what is taught in a ברייתא:
"And for it he sets his soul":
for what reason did this one climb up a ramp
and hang from a tree
and hand himself over to death?
Was it not for his wages?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 1.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק explains why the wages must be paid: the worker risks his life to earn them.

steps.title: Withholding wages is like taking a soul
steps.stepSummary: A second reading of the same פסוק: anyone who withholds a שכיר's wages is as if he takes a soul.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another explanation: "For he sets his soul upon it" means that whoever withholds a hired worker's wages is as if he takes his soul from him.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a second way to read the same words. Withholding a worker's pay is compared to taking his life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first reading was about what the worker gives, which is his risk of life. This reading is about what the employer does, which is like taking a נפש. The phrase "his soul" is unclear, and that sets up the next step's argument.

keyTerms.meaning: One who withholds or holds back (money owed).

phrases.english: Another explanation:
"And for it he sets his soul":
anyone who withholds the wages of a hired worker
is as if he takes his soul from him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second reading of the same פסוק from the ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Withholding a שכיר's wages is like taking a נפש.

steps.title: Whose soul: the robber's or the victim's?
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא and רב חסדא disagree: one says the soul taken is the גזלן's own, the other says it is the נגזל's.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא and רב חסדא disagree. One says it means the soul of the robber; the other says it means the soul of the person robbed.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים argue about whose soul the ברייתא is talking about. Is it the employer who withholds the pay, or the worker who is cheated?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If it is the גזלן's soul, it is a punishment: Heaven takes his life for this sin. If it is the נגזל's soul, it describes the harm: the worker suffers so much that it is like killing him. The גמרא does not say which אמורא holds which view.

keyTerms.meaning: A robber. Here, the employer who withholds wages.
The one who was robbed. Here, the worker.

phrases.english: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda:
one says: the soul of the robber,
and one says: the soul of the one robbed.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב הוּנָא וְרַב חִסְדָּא, חַד אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the unclear word "his soul" from step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is a מחלוקת over whether the soul taken is the גזלן's or the נגזל's.
steps.confusionAlert: In the robber's view, the robber doesn't take anyone's soul. His own soul is taken from him by Heaven as punishment.

steps.title: Proof that it is the robber's soul
steps.stepSummary: The one who says "the robber's soul" brings פסוקים in משלי: God will take the soul of those who rob the poor.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one who says the robber's soul relies on: "Do not rob the poor because he is poor, and do not crush the needy in the gate," followed by "For God will fight their fight and will rob the soul of those who rob them."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the source for the first view. The פסוק says God will take the soul of whoever robs the poor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second פסוק says God ״קָבַע אֶת קֹבְעֵיהֶם נָפֶשׁ״, which means He robs the robbers of their life. So the soul that is lost is the גזלן's own, as a punishment.

keyTerms.meaning: Robbed or took away (an unusual word for stealing).

phrases.english: The one who says the soul of the robber:

phrases.aramaic: דִּכְתִיב: ״אַל תִּגְזׇל דַּל כִּי דַל הוּא
phrases.english: as it is written: "Do not rob the poor because he is poor,
and do not crush the needy in the gate,"
and it is written: "For God will fight their fight
and will rob the soul of those who rob them."

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאן דְּאָמַר נַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁל גַּזְלָן, דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the first opinion in step 4.
steps.raayaObject: That the soul taken is the גזלן's own.

steps.title: Proof that it is the victim's soul
steps.stepSummary: The one who says "the victim's soul" brings a פסוק in משלי: greed takes the life of its owners.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one who says the victim's soul relies on: "So are the ways of everyone who is greedy for gain; it takes the soul of its owners."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the source for the second view. The פסוק says greedy robbery takes the life of "its owners," meaning the people whose money it was.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This view reads ״בְּעָלָיו״ as the rightful owners of the money, who are the victims. So the robber is taking the נגזל's life.

phrases.english: And the one who says the soul of the one robbed:
as it is written: "So are the ways of everyone greedy for gain:
it takes the soul of its owners."

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַאן דְּאָמַר נַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁל נִגְזָל, דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the second opinion in step 4.
steps.raayaObject: That the soul taken is the נגזל's.

steps.title: Challenge to the robber's-soul view from the victim's verse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the first view: the פסוק plainly says "the soul of its owners" is taken.
steps.simpleTranslation: And for the other Sage too, isn't it written: "it takes the soul of its owners"?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the Sage who says the robber's soul is taken. How does he handle the פסוק that seems to say the owners lose their soul?
steps.deeperAnalysis: ״בְּעָלָיו״ sounds like the rightful owners, who are the victims. That seems to support only the second view, so the first view needs a way to read it.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it written? (opens a challenge from a פסוק)

phrases.english: And the other one too,
phrases.notes: Here "the other one" means the Sage who said it is the robber's soul.

phrases.english: isn't it written: "it takes the soul of its owners"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the second view's פסוק against the first view.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that the soul taken is the גזלן's.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: ״בְּעָלָיו״ seems to mean the victims, so the פסוק says the victim's soul is taken.

steps.title: "Its owners" means the current owner, the robber
steps.stepSummary: The first view reads ״בְּעָלָיו״ as the money's present owner, which is the robber himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: Its current owners.
steps.whatsHappening: The answer: "its owners" means whoever holds the money now, and that is the robber. So the פסוק fits the first view after all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the robber takes the money, he is in a sense its owner now. The פסוק says the stolen money ends up taking his life. So the same פסוק now supports the robber's-soul view.

phrases.english: Its owners of now.
phrases.notes: He means the robber, who now holds the stolen money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of a word in the פסוק.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: ״בְּעָלָיו״ means the original owners, the victims.
steps.terutzMaskana: ״בְּעָלָיו״ means the current holder, the גזלן.

steps.title: Challenge to the victim's-soul view from the robber's verse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the second view: the פסוק says God takes the soul of the robbers.
steps.simpleTranslation: And for the other Sage too, isn't it written: "and will rob the soul of those who rob them"?
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא challenges the Sage who says the victim's soul is taken. How does he read the פסוק that says God will take the robbers' soul?
steps.deeperAnalysis: ״וְקָבַע אֶת קֹבְעֵיהֶם נָפֶשׁ״ sounds like the robbers lose their lives. That seems to back only the first view.

phrases.english: And the other one too,
phrases.notes: This time it means the Sage who said it is the victim's soul.

phrases.english: isn't it written: "and will rob the soul of those who rob them"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Mirrors step 7 and turns the first view's פסוק against the second view.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that the soul taken is the נגזל's.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק says the robbers' soul is taken, which suggests the soul lost is the גזלן's.

steps.title: The verse gives the reason: the robbers took a soul
steps.stepSummary: The second view reads the פסוק as giving a reason: God punishes the robbers because they took a soul.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is telling us a reason: why will God rob those who rob them? Because they took a soul.
steps.whatsHappening: The answer: the word ״נָפֶשׁ״ explains why the robbers are punished. They are punished because they took the victim's soul. So this פסוק also fits the victim's-soul view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase is read as "He robs the robbers, because they took a נפש." The פסוק still describes the robbery as taking the victim's life, and the robbers' punishment is the result. With this, both views can read both פסוקים, and the מחלוקת stands.

keyTerms.meaning: It is saying a reason (the פסוק explains why).

steps.whatToRemember: Withholding a שכיר's pay is compared to taking a life. רב הונא and רב חסדא argue whether this means the robber loses his own life as punishment or the victim is "killed" by the theft. Each side can explain both פסוקים in משלי.

phrases.english: It is saying "what is the reason":
what is the reason He "robs those who rob them"?
Because they took a soul.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the פסוק's structure as giving a reason.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: ״נָפֶשׁ״ is the robbers' soul that God takes.
steps.terutzMaskana: ״נָפֶשׁ״ is the victim's soul that the robbers took, which is why God punishes them.

steps.title: The prohibition applies only when the worker asks for his pay
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: the employer violates the prohibition only if the worker claimed his wages.
steps.simpleTranslation: When does he violate it? When the worker asked him for the pay. If the worker did not ask, he does not violate it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the משנה and quotes its next line about when the employer is guilty of delaying wages. This sets up the ברייתא that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה limits the prohibition. Holding back wages is only a sin when the worker actually asked for his money. If the worker stayed quiet, the employer has not done anything wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: He claimed it from him, meaning the worker asked for his pay
He does not violate the prohibition

phrases.english: When? At a time that he claimed it from him.
phrases.notes: This is the משנה again. "He claimed it" means the worker asked the employer for his wages.

phrases.english: If he did not claim it from him, he does not transgress it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the side discussion about the robber's soul and returns to the משנה's rules on wages.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The prohibition of delaying wages is violated only if the worker asked for payment.

steps.title: A ברייתא learns from ״אִתְּךָ״ that the worker must ask
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא shows the source for the משנה's rule: ״אִתְּךָ״ means the delay must happen with the employer's knowledge, after the worker asked.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: ״The wages of a worker shall not stay overnight.″ You might think this applies even if he did not ask. So the פסוק says ״with you,״ meaning with your knowledge.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that gives the פסוק source for the rule we just read in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא first suggests the prohibition might apply even when the worker never asked. Then it uses the extra word ״אִתְּךָ״ to show the employer must know that the worker wants his pay now. If the worker did not ask, the employer is not holding back anything against the worker's wishes.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not leave it overnight. This is the prohibition of delaying wages.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
"The wages of a hired worker shall not remain overnight"
One might think: even if he did not claim it from him.
So the verse says "with you": meaning with your knowledge.
phrases.notes: The word ״אִתְּךָ״ comes later in the same פסוק: "shall not stay with you until morning."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the פסוק source for the משנה's rule in step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ״אִתְּךָ״ teaches that the employer is guilty only when he knows the worker wants his pay, after the worker has asked.

steps.title: No violation if the employer has no money
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא learns a second limit from ״אִתְּךָ״: the employer is guilty only if he actually has the money.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might think he is guilty even if he has no money. So the פסוק says ״with you,״ meaning the money is with you.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues and reads the same word ״אִתְּךָ״ a second way, to exempt an employer who has no money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here ״אִתְּךָ״ means the money is actually in your hands. An employer who cannot pay is not holding back wages, so he does not violate the prohibition.

keyTerms.meaning: That you have it with you

phrases.english: One might think: even if he does not have money.
So the verse says "with you": meaning that there is money with you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second limit, learned from the same word ״אִתְּךָ״.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An employer who has no money to pay does not violate the prohibition.

steps.title: No violation if payment was sent through a storekeeper or money changer
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא learns a third limit: if the employer arranged for a storekeeper or money changer to pay the worker, he does not violate the prohibition.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might think he is guilty even if he sent the worker to a storekeeper or a money changer for payment. So the פסוק says ״with you,״ and not when he sent him to a storekeeper or money changer.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes with a third reading of ״אִתְּךָ״. It exempts an employer who handed the payment over to someone else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The prohibition applies only while the payment is still with the employer himself. Once he arranges for a storekeeper or money changer to pay the worker, the debt is no longer held up "with you." So the employer does not violate the prohibition.

keyTerms.meaning: He transferred him. This means he directed the worker to collect from someone else.

steps.whatToRemember: ״אִתְּךָ״ teaches three limits. The worker must ask for his pay, the employer must have the money, and the payment must not have been passed on to a storekeeper or money changer.

phrases.english: One might think: even if he transferred him
to a storekeeper or to a money changer,
so the verse says "with you"

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא שֶׁהִמְחָהוּ אֵצֶל חֶנְוָנִי וְאֵצֶל שׁוּלְחָנִי.
phrases.english: and not where he transferred him to a storekeeper or to a money changer.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָכוֹל אֲפִילּוּ הִמְחָהוּ אֵצֶל חֶנְוָנִי וְאֵצֶל שׁוּלְחָנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds the third and final limit learned from ״אִתְּךָ״.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Once the employer arranges for a storekeeper or money changer to pay the worker, he does not violate the prohibition.

steps.title: The משנה: a transfer to a storekeeper or money changer exempts him
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's line that if the employer transferred payment to a storekeeper or money changer, he does not violate the prohibition.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he transferred him to a storekeeper or to a money changer, he does not violate it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes another line of the משנה. This sets up a new question about this case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We already know the employer does not sin in this case. But the משנה only says he does not violate the prohibition. It does not say whether he still owes the money if the storekeeper never pays.

phrases.english: If he transferred him to a storekeeper or to a money changer,
he does not transgress.

steps.triggerLanguage: הִמְחָהוּ אֵצֶל חֶנְוָנִי וְאֵצֶל שׁוּלְחָנִי – אֵינוֹ עוֹבֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the משנה's wording on the case the ברייתא just covered.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An employer who transfers payment to a storekeeper or money changer does not violate the prohibition.

steps.title: Can the worker go back to the employer?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if the storekeeper or money changer did not pay, can the worker go back and collect from the employer?
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: does he go back to the employer, or does he not go back?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a question about the משנה's case. If the third party never paid, can the worker return to the employer for his money?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether the transfer cancels the employer's debt completely, or only frees him from the sin of delaying wages. If the debt still exists, the worker can go back to him.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was raised before them
He goes back. Here it means the worker returns to the employer to collect.

steps.confusionAlert: Nobody here is asking whether the employer sinned. Everyone agrees he did not. The question is only about money: does the employer still owe the wages?

phrases.english: A dilemma was raised before them:
Does he return, or does he not return?
phrases.notes: "He" is the worker. If the storekeeper didn't pay, can he come back to the employer to collect?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a point the משנה in step 15 leaves open.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: After a transfer to a storekeeper or money changer, does the employer still owe the worker if the third party does not pay?

steps.title: רב ששת and רבה disagree
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת says the worker cannot go back to the employer, and רבה says he can.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said: he does not go back. רבה said: he goes back.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים answer the question in opposite ways.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ששת holds that the transfer ends the employer's responsibility completely. רבה holds that the employer still owes the money, even though he did not sin.

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said: he does not return,
and Rabba said: he returns.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives two opposite answers to the question in step 16.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב ששת: the worker cannot go back to the employer. רבה: the worker can go back to the employer.

steps.title: רבה proves his view from the משנה's wording
steps.stepSummary: רבה points out that the משנה only says the employer "does not transgress," which suggests the worker can still go back to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: How do I know this? Because the משנה says "he does not transgress." Transgressing is what he does not do, but the worker does go back to him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה brings a proof for his view from the exact words of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only says the employer is free of the sin. If the transfer had cancelled the debt completely, the משנה would have said so. So רבה concludes the debt is still there, and the worker can come back to collect.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do I say this?
From the fact that it teaches

phrases.english: Rabba said: From where do I say it?
From the fact that it teaches: "he does not transgress it,"
it is transgressing that he does not do,
but going back, he does go back.
phrases.notes: The worker can still return to the employer to collect his wages.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבה supports his side of the dispute in step 17.
steps.raayaObject: רבה's view that the worker can go back to the employer
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה says only "אֵינוֹ עוֹבֵר." This suggests only the sin is removed, not the debt.

steps.title: רב ששת reads "does not transgress" differently
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת explains that "he does not transgress" means the employer is no longer in a position to transgress at all, because he has no more responsibility.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said: What does "he does not transgress" mean? It means he is no longer someone who can transgress.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת answers רבה's proof by explaining the משנה's words another way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה read "does not transgress" as removing only the sin. רב ששת reads it as saying the employer is completely outside the prohibition, because the debt is no longer his. So the משנה's wording does not prove that the worker can go back.

keyTerms.meaning: In the category of transgressing, meaning in a position where he could transgress

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides agree the employer does not sin after a transfer. They argue about whether he still owes the money. רבה says yes, so the worker can go back. רב ששת says no, so the worker cannot.

phrases.english: And Rav Sheshet said:
What does "he does not transgress" mean?
He is not in the category of transgressing.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַב שֵׁשֶׁת אָמַר: מַאי אֵינוֹ עוֹבֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבה's proof from step 18 by reading the same words another way.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: רבה's inference from the words "אֵינוֹ עוֹבֵר"
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: "אֵינוֹ עוֹבֵר" can mean the employer is completely outside the prohibition, not just free of the sin while still owing the money.

steps.title: Does a contractor's pay fall under the ban on delaying wages?
steps.stepSummary: The Sages ask רב ששת whether an employer who hired someone through קבלנות violates בל תלין.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked רב ששת: with a contractor, does the employer violate the ban on delaying pay, or does he not violate it?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question is put to רב ששת. Until now we spoke about a worker paid by time. Now the question is about a contractor, who is paid for finishing a whole job.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule of בל תלין clearly covers a regular hired worker. A contractor is different because he is paid for a finished product, not for his hours. So it is unclear whether his pay counts as 'wages' at all.

keyTerms.meaning: Contract work, where the worker is paid for finishing a job and not by the hour
The ban on keeping a worker's pay overnight

phrases.english: They asked Rav Sheshet:
With contract work, does one violate the ban of 'do not keep overnight',
or does one not violate the ban of 'do not keep overnight'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new question after the discussion about transferring pay to a storekeeper or money changer.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether בל תלין applies when the worker is a contractor.

steps.title: The root of the question: does a craftsman own the improvement he makes?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains what the question depends on. If an אומן owns the שבח כלי, the money owed to him is a הלואה. If he does not, it is שכירות.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does a craftsman acquire the improvement of the item, so that the money is a loan? Or does a craftsman not acquire the improvement of the item, so that the money is a wage?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out the two sides of the question, so we can see what is really being asked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Side one: the craftsman owns the added value, so the owner is in effect buying it from him. That makes the money a debt or loan, and בל תלין does not apply to loans. Side two: the craftsman owns nothing, so he is just a worker and the money is a wage, which is covered by בל תלין.

keyTerms.meaning: The added value of the item that comes from the craftsman's work
A loan or debt, which is not covered by בל תלין
Wages, which are covered by בל תלין

steps.confusionAlert: Nobody actually lent anything here. 'Loan' just means that if the craftsman owns the improvement, the money owed to him is treated like an ordinary debt and not like a wage.

phrases.english: Does a craftsman acquire the improvement of the item,
so that it is a loan?

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ אֵין אוּמָּן קוֹנֶה בִּשְׁבַח כְּלִי,
phrases.english: Or does a craftsman not acquire the improvement of the item,
so that it is a wage?

steps.triggerLanguage: אוּמָּן קוֹנֶה בִּשְׁבַח כְּלִי, וְהַלְוָאָה הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind the question in step 20.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether an אומן acquires the שבח כלי, which decides if his pay counts as a loan or as a wage.

steps.title: רב ששת: the employer does violate
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת answers that the employer of a contractor does violate בל תלין.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said to them: He violates!
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת gives his answer: yes, delaying a contractor's pay breaks the ban.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the logic of step 21, this means a contractor's pay counts as a real wage, at least for the purpose of בל תלין.

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said to them: He violates!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from steps 20 and 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: An employer who hires a contractor violates בל תלין if he delays the pay.

steps.title: Challenge: a ברייתא says he does not violate
steps.stepSummary: The questioners point to a ברייתא that says a contractor's employer does not violate בל תלין.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it was taught in a ברייתא: he does not violate!
steps.whatsHappening: The questioners attack רב ששת's answer using a ברייתא that seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a ברייתא rules that there is no violation with a contractor, רב ששת's ruling seems to go directly against an earlier source.

phrases.english: But it was taught: he does not violate!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב ששת's answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's ruling that the employer of a contractor violates בל תלין.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא openly states that there is no violation for a contractor.

steps.title: Answer: the ברייתא is about pay transferred to a storekeeper
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת explains that the ברייתא is speaking about an employer who transferred the pay to a חנווני or שולחני.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, it is where he transferred the payment to a storekeeper or a money changer.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת answers the challenge. He limits the ברייתא to a special case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא's 'he does not violate' is not about contractors in general. It is about the case from the משנה, where the employer arranged for a storekeeper or money changer to pay. In that case there is no violation for any kind of worker.

keyTerms.meaning: He transferred the payment to someone else

phrases.english: There, it is where he transferred him
phrases.notes: This is the same case as in the משנה we saw in step 15.

phrases.english: to a storekeeper or to a money changer.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם שֶׁהִמְחָהוּ אֵצֶל חֶנְוָנִי וְאֵצֶל שׁוּלְחָנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the ברייתא to a specific case (אוקימתא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא exempts every contractor from בל תלין.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא only exempts an employer who transferred the pay to a storekeeper or money changer. Otherwise a contractor's employer does violate.

steps.title: A suggested proof from a garment given to a craftsman
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that a ברייתא about a טלית given to an אומן supports רב ששת, because it says the owner violates once the sun sets after the garment is returned.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us say this supports him: If someone gives his garment to a craftsman, and the craftsman finished it and told him, even from now until ten days, the owner does not violate the ban. If the craftsman gave it back to him at midday, once the sun sets on him he violates the ban.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that seems to back up רב ששת's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A craftsman who works on a garment is a type of contractor. The ברייתא's second case says that once the garment is back with the owner and the sun sets, the owner violates בל תלין. That fits רב ששת's view that a contractor's pay is covered by the ban. In the first case, while the garment is still with the craftsman, there is no violation even after many days.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us say this supports him
He finished it and told him

steps.confusionAlert: 'נימא' means 'let us say.' It is only a suggested proof, and the גמרא may still question it.

phrases.english: Let us say this supports him:
One who gives his garment to a craftsman,
and he finished it and told him,
even from now until ten days,
he does not violate the ban of 'do not keep overnight'.
If he gave it to him at midday,
once the sun has set on him
he violates the ban of 'do not keep overnight'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that the challenge is answered, the גמרא looks for support for רב ששת.
steps.raayaObject: רב ששת's ruling that a contractor's employer violates בל תלין.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that says the owner of a garment violates בל תלין once the sun sets after the craftsman returns it to him.

steps.title: Finishing the proof: why would the owner violate if the craftsman owned the improvement?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא completes the proof from the ברייתא. If an אומן owned the שבח כלי, the owner would not violate בל תלין, since the payment would be a purchase or a loan and not wages.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say that a craftsman acquires through the improvement of the item, why does the owner violate?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out the logic behind the proof it started in the last step. If the craftsman owned the improvement, the ברייתא's ruling that the owner violates בל תלין would make no sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 21 taught that if an אומן owns the שבח כלי, what he is owed is a הלואה and not wages, so בל תלין would not apply. The ברייתא says the owner does violate. So the ברייתא must hold that an אומן does not own the שבח כלי, and that backs up רב ששת.

keyTerms.meaning: A craftsman who works on someone else's item
Acquires (gains ownership) through the improvement he adds to the item
Violates (here, the prohibition of בל תלין)

phrases.english: And if you say
a craftsman acquires through the improvement of the item
why does he violate?
phrases.notes: "He" is the owner of the garment, who the ברייתא says violates בל תלין once the sun sets.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אָמְרַתְּ אוּמָּן קוֹנֶה בִּשְׁבַח כְּלִי אַמַּאי עוֹבֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the reasoning of the proof begun in step 25
steps.raayaObject: רב ששת's view that a contractor's employer violates בל תלין, because an אומן does not own the שבח כלי
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of the טלית given to an אומן, which says the owner violates once the garment is returned and the sun sets

steps.title: רב מרי: the ברייתא may be about a coarse garment that gains no improvement
steps.stepSummary: רב מרי בריה דרב כהנא rejects the proof. The ברייתא may be speaking about cleaning a thick, coarse garment, where the work adds no real improvement to own.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מרי, son of רב כהנא, said: The ברייתא is speaking about the scraping (cleaning) of a coarse garment.
steps.whatsHappening: רב מרי pushes back on the proof. He says the ברייתא could be about a kind of work that adds no improvement at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Whether an אומן owns the שבח כלי only matters if there is an improvement to own. If the work adds nothing, the craftsman owns nothing, so the owner violates בל תלין no matter which view is right. That means the ברייתא proves nothing about the general question.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב מָרִי בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב כָּהֲנָא:
phrases.english: רב מרי, son of רב כהנא, said:
With the scraping (cleaning) of a coarse garment.
phrases.notes: His point is that this kind of work does not really improve the garment, so there is no improvement for the craftsman to own.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב מָרִי בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב כָּהֲנָא בִּגְרָדָא דְּסַרְבָּלָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of steps 25-26 by narrowing the case of the ברייתא
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the ברייתא of the טלית in support of רב ששת
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא may be about work that adds no שבח, so it says nothing about whether an אומן owns the שבח

steps.title: But softening the garment is itself an improvement
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב מרי. The owner gave the garment to be softened, and that softening is exactly the improvement.
steps.simpleTranslation: For what purpose did he give it to him? To soften it. That is its improvement!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב מרי's answer. Even a coarse garment is handed over so that it will come back softer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב מרי claimed there was no improvement. The גמרא answers that softening is the whole point of the job, and a softer garment is an improved garment. So there is a שבח after all, and the question of ownership comes right back.

phrases.english: For what purpose did he give it to him?
To soften it; that is its improvement!

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמַאי יַהֲבֵהּ נִיהֲלֵיהּ לְרַכּוֹכֵי הַיְינוּ שְׁבָחֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב מרי's rejection in step 27
steps.kashyaTarget: רב מרי's claim that cleaning a coarse garment adds no improvement
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The garment was given to be softened, and softening is a real improvement, so the craftsman would own a שבח after all

steps.title: Paid a coin per tread, he is a hired worker
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the case is where the craftsman was hired to tread on the garment and was paid a מעה for each tread. He is paid for his actions, not for the result, so he is a regular hired worker.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a case where he hired him to tread on it, a מעה for each tread.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב מרי's rejection by describing the ברייתא's case more exactly. The craftsman was paid per tread, not for a finished, softened garment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A contractor is paid for the result, so the question of owning the שבח comes up. Here the worker is paid for each action he does, which makes him a שכיר, a regular hired worker. He has no claim on the improvement, so the owner violates בל תלין on any view. That leaves the ברייתא no proof for רב ששת.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for (a specific case)
To tread or stamp on a garment in water to soften it

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא of the טלית does not prove רב ששת's view. It can be read as a case where the worker was paid per action, so he is a regular hired worker, and בל תלין applies no matter who owns the שבח כלי.
steps.confusionAlert: The softened garment is still improved here. The point is not that there is no שבח, but that a worker paid per tread is not a contractor, so the ownership question never comes up.

phrases.english: No, it is needed
where he hired him to tread on it
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets; the meaning stays the same.

phrases.english: a מעה coin for each and every tread.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא דְּקָא אַגְרֵיהּ לְבַטּוֹשֵׁי בִּטְשָׁא וּבִטְשָׁא בְּמָעֲתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 28 and upholds רב מרי's rejection
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא) to a worker paid per action
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Softening is an improvement, so the craftsman would own a שבח and the ownership question would apply
steps.terutzMaskana: Since he is paid per tread, he is a regular hired worker. The owner violates בל תלין on any view, so the ברייתא is no proof for רב ששת
